utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, good morning, everyone. Mr. Hannis, outstanding matters from yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, if I may. There was an issue regarding some transcript pages that Mr. Cepic had wanted to tender. I've reviewed those. I have no objections to those.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Do you intend to ask us to take account of additional pages?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, I don't think it's necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well. We'll admit from 5D80 from pages 5452, 54 -- and from 83, 84, 89 to 91, 96, 97, and then 5499 to 5510.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Two other matters with regard to Mr. Merovci. Your Honour, there were some documents on our exhibit list that I would like to tender from the bar table in connection with him. One is Exhibit P1851, which is a Politika newspaper article from the 28th of February, 1989, reporting on the special measures just to corroborate and set a date in connection with those; then I have P859 which is an Official Gazette of Serbia on the programme for establishment of peace, liberty, equality, democracy, and prosperity in Kosovo from the 30th of March, 1990. Exhibit P1854, also from the Official Gazette of Serbia, the law on action of republican agencies under special circumstances from 16th June, 1996 [sic]. 1855, the decision on determining that special circumstances have been introduced on the territory of Kosovo, also from 26th June, 1990. 1861, the law on labour relations under special circumstances from the 26th of July, 1990. And, finally, P809, the declaration on adhere erns on provisions to the decision of taking interim measures from the 20th of October, 1991. I advised Defence counsel by e-mail last night of my intention to make this submission, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Do these all relate to the evidence of the last witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. He talked about special circumstances and special measures. They all relate to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: We have objection, Your Honour, and I will -- I mean, it's a short submission, but I would speak in Serbian with your permission. [Interpretation] The objection consists of two objections. One is very concrete and the other one is an objection in principle. The Defence believes that the Prosecution was obligated to inform us that they would ask admission for these documents before the witness came. If the Prosecution had intended to have these documents admitted through the previous witness, they should have examined the witness on the documents that they wished to admit and they want to do so after the witness has left. If they had examined the witness, the -- that would have enabled the Defence to cross-examine the witness. Based on the witness's testimony, I dare say that the witness was not explicit enough to show us that his testimony referred to precisely these documents and these issues. That is why it would be necessary for the Defence to check these allegations with the witness. As for the matter of principle, on several occasions the Defence has submitted on several occasions that it deems unacceptable, given the time in the indictment, which is the years 1998 and 1999, that the Prosecution proposes documents on laws and regulations that have been altered, changed, or abolished in the meantime. All of these regulations in question were passed by a state that ceased to exist, by which these regulations stopped existing at least three or four years before the period contained in the indictment. For that reason, it is the position of the Defence that the regulations in question are not relevant for these proceedings and that they represent an unnecessary burden for these proceedings. On the other hand, they put the Defence in a position in which the Defence will be duty-bound to provide its answers and to present evidence in that sense, which again will extend and expand the number of Defence exhibits proposed by the Defence, and this in turn will prolong the proceedings unnecessarily. If you look at the dates on the regulations that have been mentioned by Mr. Hannis, you will see that all the regulations, save for the last one that dates from the 1991, were passed before the constitution of Serbia was passed in 1990. Not even mentioned that in the meantime the SFRY stopped existing and became SRY on the 24th of April, 1992, which makes all of these regulations really irrelevant. I would especially like to emphasise that, pursuant to the decision of this Trial Chamber dated 10 October, only Exhibit P859 is contained within that decision. It is the only piece of evidence on bar table; and from that point of view, none of the others should be admitted based on that foundation, on those grounds. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Do I understand you to be saying that's already submit admitted?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No, no, no -- well, yes. That's one of the -- I'm not sure, Your Honour. I don't have the decision --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What is the order of the 10th of October? Excuse me for not remembering its precise terms, Mr. Zecevi.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That is the order on the admission of agreed facts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's the order that has not been presented to the Trial Chamber; is that the position? Or was there an order made on the 10th of October about agreed facts?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And only one of the documents on this list offered by Mr. Hannis this morning has been mentioned in that -- in that order --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And did that order admit the document?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I would presume that -- yes. Yes, that order admits that document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So that one is out.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But in relation to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But the other ones, 1854, 55, 61, and 809, these are official publications. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, can you give me an example of how you might have cross-examined the witness if you had been alerted to this prior to his evidence. Give me something that you would have had to ask him so that I can put in context the difficulty that you are referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Very easily, Your Honour. I would present the witness with the document, with the law, which is the amendment of this law or which is the law which states that these particular -- or some of these particular laws are not any more in effect. That would be the basis of my cross-examination, and that would be the basis of cross-examination of my colleagues yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But this all looks like material that should be capable of agreement, including the fact that it is no longer in existence. And because the witness has given evidence, in some instance of a very vague nature about the measures and the effect of these measures on the Albanian population, it's important to us that we don't get led up the garden path by that vague evidence and that we have the actual clear terms of the changes that were made before us so that we can assess his evidence in the light of these and perhaps even decide that there's virtually no weight to be given to this stuff at all. After all, there was no objection taken to him giving evidence in that way in the course of his testimony yesterday and the day before. And, therefore, this would appear to be an attempt to put a measure of solidity into something that was nothing -- that was at times vague. And that can hardly prejudice you because you have the opportunity of making it clear, hopefully through agreement, that these laws came to an end at a particular stage. And it's open to you to propose to the Prosecution ways of modifying the impact of this in the interests of your client. That's not to say that we don't recognise that it would have been far more appropriate for you to be told before the witness gave evidence that the Prosecution were going to seek to have these documents tendered at the bar table. It's something they should have been alert to because they can see how vague the witness's evidence is in some areas on that sort of material. Now, that really covers both points, and your point about prolonging the proceedings hopefully could be dealt with by discussion. I think you know from informal communication from Mr. Dawson that we want to bring to a head the question of discussions between parties about agreed facts. And we want to know what can't be agreed, what can be agreed, and what is the middle area that might benefit from some arbitration by the Bench, and this is an example I think of what might fall into that category. So I think we would be inclined to encourage you to be looking at ways of allowing this material to be admitted, along with enough material from your part to give the full picture that you want to present. So I don't think we'll take an instant decision on this, but I don't think we would want to refuse it out of hand. We'll consider it in a moment, but I get the general feeling from my colleagues that that's the position. As far as number 1 is concerned, I need to hear from Mr. Hannis -- perhaps you have something to say about that. That's 1851. Politika is a newspaper or a -- it's part of -- it's a press publication.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: In principle, we are not happy about that sort of evidence; on the other hand, there's a measure of -- it's a more official publication than perhaps some of the other media --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- materials and would, generally speaking, not be prejudicial to the Defence, I suspect.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So you don't isolate -- you don't take this particular Politika piece as one that should just be rejected out of hand as a piece of journalism.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No, we have the objection on the whole side of these documents, and it's the very same objection which I already stated. We and the Office of the Prosecution are really working on this material, and I can assure you that the -- probably as early as next week we will have the -- our agreement with more than 350 laws which have been agreed between the parties as -- and that is, in principle, exactly the point because we -- we would be -- we would be inclined to stipulate to these laws in a package where we have this law, the amendment, and the annulment of that law because it is -- it is from the Official Gazette so there is no problem with the real -- authenticity. I'm sorry. That was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, you're not the only one who has trouble with the English language, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We will consider the position.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: There are two general things to be said about this situation. One is to express disappointment that so far into the trial we're still unclear about the areas of law and the provisions of law that can be agreed between the parties as having applied at various stages of the events that may be relevant to the indictment. The second general comment to make is to appreciate the way in which the parties have addressed the issue and to thank Mr. Zecevic for his very helpful submission on the matter because he makes very valid points in opposition; on the other hand, I think everyone must appreciate the anxiety of the Trial Chamber to have before it the official documentation in relation to matters of this nature. So what we shall do is continue consideration of the motion to admit these documents pending the stage at which we intervene, if necessary, to arbitrate on the attempt by parties to reach agreement on very -- on the admission of various documents. We hope our intervention will not be necessary. It may encourage your debate to know that we are generally inclined to admit this material, but we would want to do so, if we do so, in the context of the Defence presenting the additional material they feel is necessary to give it a proper understanding. And we will not make a final decision along these lines without giving you a further opportunity, if necessary, to address the matter. So hopefully within a fairly short period we will have got to the stage of addressing not only these documents but any others on which there is hope for agreement. Now, are there any other preliminary issues, Mr. Hannis?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, I just wanted to alert the Court that -- and Defence counsel that in light of some of the cross-examination of Mr. Merovci regarding Dr. Rugova's positions about certain things and in light of the rule change to Rule 92 ter, we propose that we will probably file a new submission asking the Court again to consider admitting Dr. Rugova's statement and/or testimony from Milosevic. We had done that earlier in the case under Rule 92 bis (C) and that motion was denied at the time in part because much of his testimony went to the acts and conduct of the accused. And I take from the language of the new rule, in light of how some of the evidence was presented yesterday, we will make a new argument to you. I just wanted to alert you to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I can tell you that the Chamber actually considered this question informally because if we had felt it was something we would have wanted to hear more about, then we would have raised it with you. So that may indicate that we didn't decide that this was necessarily evidence we would wish to hear; on the other hand, we are not surprised that you should consider making such a motion in light of the changed rule, but you should do so quickly because the Defence will have to respond to that and this is far from a foregone conclusion. I think this is a matter we would need to consider very carefully in view of the decision we took earlier and bearing in mind the reasons for that earlier decision. We were influenced, to some extent, in our short discussion of the matter by the fact that perhaps the motion you made earlier would have been better made after Merovci had given evidence in any event. Now, when that submission is made or when that -- if that motion is made by the Prosecution, it's the type of thing that we would invite the Defence to address immediately so that we can reduce the time for response. There's -- it's already been addressed at an earlier stage in the trial. I doubt if the issues have changed all that much, although the rules have changed; and therefore, we should be able to deal with it fairly speedily.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That's it, Your Honour, I just wanted to advise you. Now I'm ready to call our next witness, who is General Aleksandar Vasiljevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic has a matter before we bring the witness in. Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to raise an issue before we have the witness in the courtroom, and the issue is relative to his testimony. It seems to us that it would be better for us to discuss the matter before the witness is in the courtroom. In the notification dated 11 January, the Prosecution proposed that through this witness we have a number of documents admitted for which they deem that through this witness enough ground should be laid for these documents to become evidence in this case. The Defence know that witness Vasiljevic in the period that most of the documents are relative to was out of active service. As it says by the statement of the witness, he returned to active duty on the 27th of April, 1999. Up to that day, he was required, and he did not participate in any of the events that are mentioned in his statement. He was not in service. He was not in Kosovo. He does not have any immediate knowledge about the events that are described in these documents and that were issued before the 27th of April, 1999. It seems inappropriate to us to establish a link to lay enough grounds for these documents to be admitted. Your Honour, we are talking about documents which are mentioned in notification by number: P928, P929, P931, P932, P935, P938, P939, and P941. These are documents, i.e., minutes from the meetings of the Chief of Staff of Yugoslavia, and all these documents precede the time that I'm talking about. They were all issued in 1998 and the first three months of 1999, i.e., during the time when Vasiljevic was retired. He was not in active service. He did not have any ties with the army or the events that we are talking about. In addition to that documents P1418, P147 [as interpreted], P1460, P1487, P1960, P103 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel please slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] P1 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Too quick, Mr. Petrovic, please slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll apologise. I'll try and do it again. P1960 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: There's an earlier one as well. You gave us 1418 and then 147, but that's unlikely to be an accurate number. What was the second one?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment. 1427.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1427, P1960, P1487, P1967, P1503, P2031, P2113, and, finally, P2591. The second group of documents are documents of various nature which refer to the military and the police. Likewise, all of these documents go beyond the scope of time that I've been talking about, and for that reason I don't think they should be admitted. There is another -- and also P2166. I apologise. My colleague has just suggested that this document is of the same nature. There are two more documents that are disputable for the Defence, and of which this witness can't say anything. Those are documents P1468 and P1898. Those are two documents which are handwritten documents. The first one is the notes from the meeting of Joint Command, and the second document is described as a notebook by a higher officer of the Serbian MUP. With regard to these two documents, we would like to point out that these are obviously handwritten documents written by some persons, that it is not known how they were created, that the witness did not participate in any of the events that are described therein, and that for that reason he cannot authenticate these documents. And based on these documents, he cannot propose any statements or testimony. Therefore, I would kindly ask the Trial Chamber to consider our objection and does not allow for these documents to be admitted through this witness. There may be some other witnesses that the Prosecution may be calling that will be able to establish a link that will constitute the grounds for the admission of these documents. Witness Vasiljevic is certainly not such a witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, there was one document that was missed which is P1049 which is also dated from the time-period before Mr. Vasiljevic was returned to service when he was, in fact, still retired and not participating in any of the events.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What is that document, Mr. Ivetic?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That is listed as being a Djakovica SUP document listing PJP members dated the 8th April, 1999. I'm told there's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, if you look at page 12 of the transcript, line 16, there's a reference to 2166. Was that, in fact, 1266?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this is 2166, and the argument that can be applied is the same. It is on page 5 of the notification dated 11 January, the same notification that I've already mentioned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It was a simply a clarification of the number I sought. Yes, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: One other matter, Your Honour, in addition to the documents that are listed in the notification, yesterday morning we received additional documents for the first time being linked to this witness. One is P1996 meeting notes or minutes of a meeting held on the -- of the MUP staff, which the witness obviously did not participate in and did not have any -- I don't see how he can testify as to it. And I would also object to the disclosure of this document at the late time, since the witness was anticipated to give testimony yesterday that we just received this document yesterday morning at 8.00, I believe, as being linked to this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Petrovic, in relation to the first group which were minutes of the Chief of Staff of Yugoslavia, are you challenging their authenticity?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, at this point in time we, quite simply, do not know. We cannot state our views on that. We simply know and claim that this witness cannot say anything about it because he did not take part in any of it. He was retired. This is beyond his knowledge. He cannot say anything about that. At this point in time, on the basis of what we know, we cannot state any position on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can we please have P928 on e-court. There's an English version on the screen. Can we have the original, and can we have the last page of that original, please. Mr. Hannis, is that an original document or is that a copy that's been made from an original document?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, these are documents that the Prosecution received from the Government of Serbia and Montenegro in response to request for assistance for these very items, for the minutes of the VJ collegium. I note on the cover, Your Honour, you may want to look in the English, it describes them as being the - let me get the wording correctly --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Let's go back to the first page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes. They're described as unauthorised and unrevised audio transcript of the decision on the particular day, but we received no other information in response to these RFAs. We received no audiotapes, we received no signed copies, we received nothing indicating that it was revised. This is the sum total of the response to that RFA for these particular items. We would continue our argument -- we would argue to the Court that that should go to weight and not admissibility. These are from the party opponent, basically.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The objection may have two bases. The one that's been stated, which is that this shouldn't be admitted at this stage because the authenticity is not established, we can look at that question; and the other basis may be this witness, any questions put to this witness about the document should not be allowed because he's not in a position to deal with them. Now, what's your answer to the second point?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, the evidence will be that General Vasiljevic was a career soldier. He was prematurely retired in 1992, reactivated again in late April 1999. In his earlier term of service, he had actually been a sitting participant in VJ collegium proceedings in 1992. It's my understanding that the VJ collegium is something that was a regular part of the General Staff. The head of the General Staff had these meetings on a weekly basis, sometimes more often. So he's familiar with the process, and indeed he's familiar with the participants because these are other generals that he went to the service with. He can provide comments about the participants and he can provide, we say, Your Honour, he can provide comments about some of the substance of the discussions that were going on, not because he was present but because he knows the participants and because he has knowledge of the events at the time they were occurring even though he was retired. His brain was not turned off, his eyes were not closed, he was aware of events that were happening, he maintained contacts with his fellow soldiers, and he was advised of some things after the events by colleagues which puts him in a position to comment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Staying with this example, how would it come into the evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, our position is that because these are received from the government as --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, give me the context of your examination of the witness that would bring this document in.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well -- okay, Your Honour. One of the issues in this case is whether or not a Joint Command existed; another is whether or not there was a Supreme Command. There will be references in the documents that refer to those two bodies and that will support his position that there indeed was a Joint Command, and it will corroborate his evidence about a Supreme Command that he dealt with after he was re-activated. And it establishes, we say, the existence of those bodies at a time prior to his re-activation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Now, can we now have on the screen P1418.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, if --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: If you want to move to that next exhibit, that's fine, but I would want to make some submissions in response to what Mr. Hannis just said about being able to bring the witness in and ask for his comments on participants and that sort of thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, but that doesn't go to the admissibility of the document, Mr. O'Sullivan; it goes to whether the questions ought to be allowed, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And that, I think, is a matter that's going to have to arise -- be dealt with at and when the questions arise. You, Mr. Petrovic, is this a good example of the second category of documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Are you challenging the authenticity of this document and the others in this category?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, my answer is the same, as in respect to the first category of documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Let me ask Mr. Aleksic, do you challenge the authenticity of this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm not challenging the authenticity of this document, but I can subscribe to what my colleague Mr. Petrovic said with regard to the first group of documents that this witness was not in active military service and, as Mr. Hannis said, his mind was working and so on and so forth. He can only have indirect knowledge about this if any. And I think in his statement --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, I understand that point. At the moment I'm concerned to establish the extent to which the documents themselves may be challenged. I entirely accept that there may be valid objections taken to questions that are asked of the witness, which is the second separate point which hasn't really been focussed by Mr. Petrovic but which may be the essence of the objection. The concern of the Trial Chamber at the moment is to identify the extent to which there's a dispute about authenticity. So thank you for that. Mr. Ivetic, I'm told that a number of these documents are police documents. Those that are police documents, are you challenging their authenticity?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I believe some of them I am. One of the documents, the one I mentioned as 1049, it's actually 1249. There was an error of the OTP's notification. That document has already, I believe, come in through another witness. I just think that it's improper to utilise that with this particular witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, that's a question we can address when the questions are asked, but I'm concerned at the moment about the second category of document. And Mr. Petrovic said that they consisted of military and police documents outwith the period of service of the witness. Now, those that are police documents. Do you dispute their authenticity?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I don't believe there are any police documents in that batch, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And you added to the list for concern P1996. Is that document -- is that the authenticity of that document in dispute?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I do not believe so, Your Honour, no, not by us at least.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So is your objection fairly technical? I take the point about notice.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: It's the utilisation of that document with this witness. I think that may have come in actually with another witness as well, from my recollection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Hannis, two final questions. Is P1418 a good example of all of these that fall under the second category do you know? Are they all of this nature with a signature and a stamp?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Almost all, Your Honour. There are some Joint Command orders that are not signed or stamped.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Are they -- so they may fall into the second category as well. The Joint Command documents are not all in the first category?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. Some of those were not signed or stamped, but they were received pursuant to an RFA.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And my second question relates to the two final documents referred to by Mr. Petrovic, both handwritten. One was a note from the meeting of the Joint Command and another was a notebook of a higher officer of the MUP, neither of them being linked to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What's the basis for --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'll take --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- introducing them through the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'll take the last one first, Your Honour, and again we say there is evidence regarding their authenticity based on the source. And we're asking -- we're going to ask this witness to comment on certain aspects of the contents of those. The last one, the notebook of a high official in the MUP, was an exhibit in the Milosevic case. And General Obrad Stevanovic came here and testified, and in the course of his testimony he indicated that that was his diary. So it has been established through the testimony of a witness in the Milosevic case that General Stevanovic was the author of that. We intend to ask General Vasiljevic some questions about a few entries in that diary a meeting about the 17th of May, 1999.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's a meeting he attended?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No. It's a meeting we believe happened the same day and had discussions related to the matters that were he discussed in the meeting that he talks about in his evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And the first one.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: The first one, it appears to be a handwritten summary or minutes of meetings of Joint Command for Kosovo and Metohija in 1998. We do not know who the author was, but it names the participants, including a couple of our accused. And we have some evidence from General Vasiljevic about the existence of that Joint Command and how it met and who the participants were. We believe that some of his evidence, in commenting on the contents, may add to the authenticity of the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What's the date of the meeting it refers to?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: It's several meetings throughout the year beginning in July 1998 throughout the end of October 1998.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And you have nothing to establish its authenticity?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, this was received pursuant to an RFA to the Government of Serbia and Montenegro for Joint Command documents. It does not have a seal or a stamp, but it was in response to that specific RFA. And we believe it is in some way self-authenticating because the contents refer to events that we know about from other sources.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. O'Sullivan.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Finally, we challenge the authenticity of P2166.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can we see that, please, on the screen. This is a skillful forgery.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: We don't concede the authenticity, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is that modification on we challenge? Sorry. You're not modifying your position? You're simply challenging the authenticity of the document. Okay. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, this was a Defence exhibit in the Milosevic case with the witness Obrad Stevanovic. It was offered by Mr. Milosevic. It is sealed and stamped and we believe it is authentic.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Well, if the Prosecution is accepting the truth and authenticity of Defence, Mr. Milosevic's defence and all his Defence witnesses, we find that very interesting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Authenticity and truth are two separate concepts, Mr. O'Sullivan.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Absolutely, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And there was no finding by the Milosevic Trial Chamber of the authenticity or the reliability of this document or the testimony of Mr. Stevanovic. And we challenge it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What is your plan for dealing with the evidence of Stevanovic in the Milosevic trial?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, my plan is only to have this witness come in on a particular entry in his diary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm not -- at this point, he's not a witness we intend to call.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: As you know, the Trial Chamber much earlier in this case decided that the fact that a document had been presented in another case did not satisfy the terms of -- is it Rule 94?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Rule 94, Your Honour. And by saying I accept the authenticity of this particular document, Your Honour, I don't mean to say I accept the authenticity of every document that was offered by Mr. Milosevic or his witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We'll consider the position.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, one point to add on the diary 1898, that was introduced in cross-examination. It's my recollection - and I don't have the Stevanovic testimony here - but it's my recollection that he also testified that the diary was out of his possession and that certain portions of it appeared to be altered. So I don't believe that his testimony can be said to vouch for the authenticity of the exhibit as a whole.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I have it noted as 1899. Is that wrong?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Again, Your Honour, I'm relying on the OTP witness notification, but I can try and find it right now. I believe it's 1898, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I believe that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's not possible for us to take a decision on this at this point in time. The documents we've looked at briefly either come from a source that is indicative of their authenticity or appear on the face of them to be authentic. We think the real meat of this objection is to the qualification or competence of the witness to address the issues that may be raised in examination about these documents, and that's something that's going to have to be addressed as and when it arises. It may be that a pattern emerges and we can make a more general decision; but until we see how they're being presented, see the context in which they are presented, we can't make a decision about whether this witness can speak about them or indeed a decision about any challenge to their authenticity. Simply because a witness was not actually in a particular post at the time a document was compiled doesn't determine necessarily whether he can comment on the contents of the document. It may be he has experience of the body which is the source of the document at a time which we consider is relevant enough to enable him to comment on documents of that body relating to a prior period in time. That remains to be seen in the context of the evidence as it's led. Now, unless there is any other preliminary matter we will proceed with the evidence. Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I have two matters from the statement which is being tendered by the -- proffered by the Prosecution into evidence. First of all, the material that was first given with respect to this witness with respect to the transcript of his interview and the transcript of the testimony was given to us at the beginning of the case. This statement dated the 26th and 27th of October, 2006, was not tendered to us until January the 9th, 2007. And for the first time now -- not only was the original statement not given to us until the 9th, but then the amendment that came on the 14th changed the original. Now for the first time, at paragraphs 62 and 81, there are things listed against Mr. Lukic individually, which appear -- did not appear in any of the prior information and, in fact, contrary indications of other persons saying the things that are alleged to have been said are contained in the other materials. So I would make a technical objection to that, based upon the past course of action that we've taken that not disclosing material and then disclosing it shortly before a witness of this magnitude is highly improper. And I would ask the OTP to be sanctioned for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Give me details in relation to these two paragraphs, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes. In paragraph 62, there's now an allegation relating to a proposed commission for investigation of crimes that it is alleged Mr. Lukic turned down participation in. And in paragraph 81, a statement is made at this meeting that had previously been identified as coming from General Djordjevic are now being attributed to General Lukic, a report on activities of some detail, which in the prior addition had been linked to Djordjevic and now is being linked to my client, again in the latest revision that came out 14th of January, which was just this past, I believe, Sunday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The trouble about this sort of thing is that it might well simply have emerged in oral examination of the witness, and both are matters which are in themselves covered by the statement -- the material as expanded in 62 and changed in 81. What's the sanction you're suggesting?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, I guess that they be -- obviously, that they be barred from presenting evidence on these two topics insofar as the disclosures that were done prior to the recess did not have this information in them and were quite extensive. We're talking about I think 985 pages of transcripts and strews and the testimony I believe it was seven days of the Milosevic case. It's a difficulty that we have been having in this case that the material that's disclosed does not comport to what we at the end of the day have to deal with when we're preparing the cross-examination. So I -- again, for the record, I think I have to make this objection, although I understand where Your Honour's -- I understand Your Honour's comments that have been made already.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The sanction for problems of this particular nature is adjournment to enable the Defence to make inquiry, if necessary. If this causes any difficulty, then we will consider favourably an application for adjournment for that purpose. Any further preliminary matters?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, just a comment on that last. I have to go back and double-check my notes, but 95 percent of this statement was based on material that was in his prior testimony or interviews. As I recall, the new materials related to some Joint Command documents that we did not have in hand when we interviewed him and when he testified and one matter regarding Stevanovic's diary. But I'll double-check. I trust that Mr. Ivetic was thorough; and if he says it wasn't in any of the other materials, he is right. But I suspect we won't get to cross-examination of Mr. Vasiljevic until Monday or Tuesday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, if any question of sanction arises, obviously you'll have had time to check whether the position as presented by Mr. Ivetic is entirely accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I do not anticipate asking for an adjournment, just so that that's clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's now have the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Vasiljevic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: When we came into court, we did not realise that there would be a number of matters to be dealt with before your evidence began. You've become controversial before you got into the courtroom; however, we have now dealt with the various issues that counsel wanted us to address prior to hearing your evidence and we are ready to begin hearing your evidence. So would you please make the solemn declaration to speak the truth by reading aloud the document which will now be placed before you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated. You will appreciate that the Trial Chamber already has before it a large amount of material that you have contributed to the work of the Tribunal. We have the relevant parts of the transcript of your evidence in the trial of Slobodan Milosevic. We have a recent statement that you gave, which is largely, I assume, similar to previous statements you've given but has been supplemented and brought up-to-date. We have read that material. The purpose of you coming here is to enable counsel to ask questions, possibly to add to the information we've got already, to clarify things, and in many instances to challenge your evidence, as you will appreciate, because we have six accused here, all represented, who undoubtedly will want to wish to challenge parts of what you've said. We're hoping that the oral part of your testimony will concentrate on the really important issues and on any additional information that needs to be presented to the Chamber. So when you're answering, please try to concentrate your answer on the particular issue that's raised in the question, bearing in mind how much we already have in front of us. There's no point in repeating what we have here. We want to concentrate on the issues that the parties see as issues that are controversial in the case. So please at the present us in that way and we'll make most rapid progress if you're able to do that. The first counsel to question you will be for the Prosecutor, and that is Mr. Hannis. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Good morning, General. My apologies to the delay in our start and my part in that. I want to begin by asking your full name for the record, please.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: Aleksandar Vasiljevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And, General, I have to begin with some preliminary paperwork. Prior to coming to testify this morning, did you this past weekend have a chance to meet with us and complete a written statement? And I'll ask the usher to hand you two documents. Did you have a chance to meet with me and other individuals from the OTP to complete and sign a statement regarding your evidence in this case?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And did you have a chance to review that and make corrections before that was done?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: The two documents you have in front of you, sir, are Exhibit P2594, which is the complete statement, and the one that is numbered P2600 is a redacted version of the same one, which has portions blacked out. And those are portions you indicated that you would like to only give evidence about in private session. Are you satisfied that those are true and accurate?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: I have not had a chance to look at all the things that are for private session, but I believe that there shouldn't be any problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And can you attest to the Court that that is your evidence and those are the answers you would give if you were asked those same questions under oath today?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: We would tender the statement, Your Honour, 2594 is the unredacted version we would like to file under seal; and 2600 is the one we tender for public filing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hannis. 2594 will be held under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, General Vasiljevic, you were at the Tribunal before in February 2003 and testified in the Milosevic case. Do you recall your testimony in that case?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: Most of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you ever have an opportunity to review any of the videotapes of your actual testimony?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And based on having done that, are you satisfied that that was a true and accurate account of your evidence in that case?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: The part that I saw was accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, we would offer in Exhibits P2589, which are the open testimony excerpts, and P2590, which are the private session or closed session excerpts from Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just one moment, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I don't know if your last question actually satisfies the rule in relation to the transcript. The real question is whether his evidence would be the same in this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I can address that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: With regard to your testimony in the Milosevic case concerning the Kosovo matters and the general background matters in your personal history, would your answer to those questions that you gave in Milosevic be the same if you were asked those questions today?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: This was four years ago, so I can't be sure of every single word, but the essence would still be the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you testify truthfully in that case?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, now I would tender.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Vasiljevic, have you any reason to doubt the accuracy of any part of the evidence you gave in the Milosevic trial?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, because I told the truth at the time to the extent I remember and given the questions that were put to me. As far as I can remember, most of my testimony was about Croatia. And, finally, the last questions were about Kosovo and I testified about that. I don't know if there is anything in dispute. You can ask me specifically and I can tell you what is accurate, what is not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hannis. We'll admit the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, General, I want to go through your statement and ask you to expand on some matters and perhaps clarify a few others.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I should indicate, Your Honour, with regard to the transcript that we ask for the 2590 to be under seal. Those are the closed session excerpts they had a separate exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Give me the numbers again, Mr. Hannis..

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And what's the number of the transcript in general, the rest of it?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, 2589 are all the open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. 2590 will be held under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, you were a career military officer and you're now retired. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: When you completed the military academy in 1961, what rank did you have when you began your active military service in the JNA?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: I was a second lieutenant.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And what branch or what part of the VJ were you a member of or specialise in?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: I was -- I completed my basic education in NBC; and after the staff academy, I became part of the infantry.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And how long were you in the infantry?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: From 1973 until the moment I was pensioned off. This was the first time in 1992 when I was pensioned off, then the second time this was in 2001.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And specifically within the infantry, was there a particular department that you worked in?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: From 1964 I worked in the security bodies. I started with basic positions and functions; and up to 1982 when I served in the Sarajevo army, there I became the chief of the army security. In 1986 I was moved to the security administration, to the counter-intelligence department, and then in 1988 I went back to Sarajevo and I became division commander. This is where I stayed for two years and then I went back to the security administration in 1990, and there I was deputy chief of that department.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us briefly what is the role and function of the security administration in the JNA and the VJ.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: The security administration was in charge, and it directed the work of security bodies in lower commands. You have to make a distinction between command and control of the work of these organs. Security organs were subordinated to the commanders of the respective units; and in professional terms within their purview, they were subordinated to a higher body of security in the superior command; that was the hierarchy along the professional lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You mentioned a distinction between command and control. Can you explain that for us.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: The activity of the security bodies is regulated by special regulations. This is counter-intelligence service and counter-intelligence service has the lowest level, that was the command of the army, i.e., the commander of the army. When it came to counter-intelligence and the issues pertaining to that area, the lowest level of command was the army command that was in charge of the work of the security bodies. The army commander approved specific measures pertaining to the purview of that service. When it came to the command chain, security officers from the battalion to the higher bodies, they functioned in the work as any other officers. They participated in the work of that command. They organised provision measures to provide security to the officer in command. You have to make a distinction between the security work per se and counter-intelligence work on the other hand.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could you explain for me the difference between security work and counter-intelligence work as it relates to the army.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: I have not received interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: The question was: Could you explain the difference between security work and counter-intelligence work as it relates to the army.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: Counter-intelligence activities consisted of monitoring foreign agents or foreign intelligence services, discovering and preventing secret organised enemy activities, and also discovering and preventing terrorist acts.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And security work?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: Security work implied the organisation of measures to provide security for the command and units, participation in the drafting of plans and combat orders, which included a security item. These would be the measures of security and general safety.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: In case you're in any doubt, Mr. Hannis, I'm totally bamboozled by all of this. It's absolutely meaningless to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I hope it will become clearer before we're finished. I'm going to move to another topic and come back to this in relation to something else, and I think it will be easier to see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, from the time that you graduated and were a second lieutenant until your eventual retirement and your rank, upon your retirement was what sort of general, what level of general?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: When I was pensioned off in May 1992, I was major-general. When I was reinstated in 1999 and then mentioned off again towards the end of 2000, I was colonel-general --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And during the --

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: -- lieutenant-general.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And during the course of your military career, did you receive any awards or were you decorated for your service?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: How many times, do you recall?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: Quite a number of times. You know how it is with decorations and awards. You receive them periodically if you are successful in your job. I also had an order of courage that I received in 1991. That is an award or decoration that doesn't belong to the general group of decorations that I received?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And to become a general in the VJ, were there any kind of special schools that you had to go to as you were being promoted up from your beginning rank of second lieutenant?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: I had to complete education after the military academy. First of all, I had to go to the command staff academy; and sometime when I became lieutenant-colonel, I had to go to the so-called war school in the JNA or the School of National Defence; however, this did not mean automatically that you would be awarded a rank. They were just a pre-condition if you were considered for a rank that you might be eligible for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In paragraph 3 of your statement you indicated that you were prematurely pensioned off in 1992. Can you explain for the Court how that happened.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: The interpretation I received was "temporarily pensioned off," whereas, I suppose you said "prematurely." I was prematurely pensioned off on the 8th of May, 1992, with a number of other generals, some 70 of JNA generals were pensioned off at the time. Why was this premature? Because the criterion was for the generals to meet certain criteria; either to be 57 years of age or to have had 40 years of service. I didn't meet any these criteria; and out of the 70 generals that were pensioned off, only two generals pentioned off without meeting the requirements, I and my deputy, Major Simeon Tumanov.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you receive any explanation about why you were chosen for early retirement?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: At that time there were no explanations given. It was just explained by the needs of the service, and that's why we were retired. In the Milosevic case, I explained the circumstances under which I was mentioned off. I can go over that again, but I don't think that is important.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me move on to paragraph 4 of your statement. You mentioned that then shortly of your retirement, in July 1992 you were arrested and charged and eventually acquitted. Can you tell us briefly what that was about.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, a total of eight security officers were arrested; I was among them. General Tumanov was also supposed to be arrested; however, at that time, he had already left for Macedonia to stay with his family. There was a scandal staged, and I was charged with abuse of my official position. It was alleged that there was an operation called Kanal, where I abused my position, and the operation was done in order to discover some arms. We were all acquitted. I was acquitted in the first instance, which was then confirmed by the Supreme Military Court. I spent four months in jail. Some of my colleagues spent some eight or nine months in jail, and we had been removed from our positions because new politics came to the scene and they had to deal with the former security services. Since I've started talking about that, I would like to remind you that on the 5th of March, 1992, Mr. Milosevic invited me to come to talk to him and the -- the essence of that conversation or an important part of that conversation was his request for me to provide him with conversation on the work of the security administration. I refused to do that. I didn't comply with that request, and this was the main portion of the reason why I was retired. When I was reinstated in 1999, again, I went to talk to Milosevic on 25 April 1999, and he wanted to leave an impression that he hadn't been informed about everything that was surrounding the -- my arrest.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me ask you one more question before we take our first break. Between your premature pensioning off in 1992 and April 1999 when you re-joined the army, you lived as a retired general, did you maintain contact with any of your army colleagues during that time?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes. I communicated after my acquittal. I would go to the administration for security where there was still officers who had previously been subordinated to me and they were correct in their behaviour towards me, and I mostly socialised with either active or retired officers, generals.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, is this a good time for the break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hannis. For technical reasons, Mr. Vasiljevic, we have to break at this stage. We'll break for about 20 minutes. The usher will show you where to wait meanwhile, so could you please leave the courtroom with him. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We'll resume at 10 minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, when we broke you mentioned that you had stayed in touch with some of your army colleagues during your retirement. During that period between 1992 and 1999 when you were reinstated, did you keep abreast of public affairs as well as what was happening with the army during those years?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In paragraph 5 of your statement, you tell us that after the NATO air-strikes began you offered your services to the army. How did you do that? Who did you contact to say, Is there something I can do? I'm willing to help.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: I was addressed by a large number of security officers who had been pensioned off in the years before that. Some had war assignments in the army and others did not. We were all willing, for patriotic reasons, to help in a way, if we could. I did not specifically seek to have any meeting in this respect in terms of my re-activation, but probably people found out. Sometime in the beginning of April, General Geza Farkas invited me, and at that time he became chief of the security administration. So I wasn't looking for him. He's the one who looked me up and he asked me then whether I would accept re-activation and appointment in the republican service of the state security, with a view to attaining some coordination between military and civilian security, and I accepted that in principle. This was in the beginning of April. However, it was only on the 25th of April that General Ojdanic informed me that I was supposed to come to the command post, that President Milosevic wanted to talk to me about my re-activation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I think you mentioned in an earlier answer that you met with Mr. Milosevic on the 25th of April. Can you tell us briefly where you met him and what you two discussed on that day.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: We met at the command post of the Supreme Command. The conversation took place only between him and me; there were no other persons present. I already mentioned that that first meeting of his with me after so many years was along the following lines: Where I had been in the meantime, what was this that had happened to me, and so on and so forth. If I need to expand on this conversation, I can say that the chief of the military security service could have even have been Bismarck and even Bismarck would have been replaced if he held that post. And if Bismarck wanted to go public, then they probably would have arrested him if he spoke to the newspapers, too. I gave an interview after that in a weekly magazine, Nin, in Belgrade, and that probably led to the fact that court proceedings were brought against me. He just left. He left the impression that he sort of did not even know about what had been happening. I gave my assessments regarding the situation in the army and also with regard to certain security personnel who had already been replaced from their positions. Before all, it was General Branko Gajic who, or rather, Colonel Branko Gajic who at that time was the deputy head of the security administration, so this was one of the key people of the service who had been replaced and envisaged for retirement; then Nikola Glumac, a colonel, was there, too. And he was chief of security in the 2nd Army in Podgorica, and there were other personnel like that. The next thing I said to him was that I went through 1991 and 1992 and that I knew what different military groups did. And I posed that specifically meaning the village of Lovas. And if I was to be reactivated even now, I wouldn't reconcile myself with that kind of situation that this mafia, if I can call it that, taint the uniform that we wear. And Milosevic said, "That's the kind of man I need." He said that I would be the deputy of the chief of security administration. Since Colonel Gajic had already been removed from that office, I did not want to take this office under such circumstances after his removal. He said, "No, you're going to be that." Because General Ojdanic, when he invited me for that conversation, he said that I was supposed to be his advisor for security because the people from state security around Milosevic did not agree that I should join their structure. So I agreed -- I disagreed that I would be this deputy, but Milosevic said, "No, you will the deputy and Gajic will be this other thing." And this other thing is assistant for counter-intelligence work. That position is called the deputy chief of the security administration, at the same time the assistant for counter-intelligence work. So Milosevic separated this one position into two. So Colonel Gajic was reinstated; and on the Army Day, on the 16th of June, he received the rank of general and I was appointed deputy.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And your specific title then was deputy of what?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: Deputy of the chief of the security administration; whereas, the chief of the security administration was General Geza Farkas, who was appointed after General Aleksandar Dimitrijevic had been removed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If I understand correctly then General Farkas at that time was the number one -- had the highest position in the security administration or the -- is it the security administration or the security service?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: The security administration is at the top of the security service. It is the top institution within the security services.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Within the army?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: Within the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And so the top-ranking security officer was General Farkas?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you, as deputy head, does that mean that you were number two?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was number two, and Colonel Gajic was two and a half, so to speak, because we shared this second-ranking office.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned that General Farkas had recently been appointed to that position to replace General Dimitrijevic, and do you know when General Dimitrijevic had been removed from the position approximately?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: I think that he had been removed sometimes in the beginning of 1999. I think it could have been the month of February. I'm not too sure about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you know why he had been replaced?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, he was replaced practically a few months after the biggest change in the military, and that was the removal of General Perisic as Chief of Staff, and then he was removed soon after that. General Dimitrijevic held that position for quite a long time because people in that position are changed after two or three years, but he was there from 1993 to 1999, that is to say all of six years. I think that he had a special kind of authority in this position as an individual, and he freely, openly expressed his views, which Milosevic did not like. As far as I know, specifically, his last clash was with regard to the way the problem of Kosovo was being resolved, and basically, that is why Perisic was removed, too, and later on Dimitrijevic as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And do you know the nature of the clash with Milosevic about Kosovo that led to Perisic being removed?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: You know what? I probably used language that was too strong when I said clash with Milosevic, hardly anyone could clash with him. But he had views that were different from his, and the reason for this was General Perisic and General Dimitrijevic also advocated the same position that a state of emergency should be used to mobilise the army because it was the MUP that was the mainstay of activity against terrorists in Kosovo. Milosevic thought that the international situation was such that such a move would not be interpreted favourably and would only further complicate the position of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and that his decision to use the army without proclaiming a state of emergency was sufficient, and that is where their views differed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you mentioned that General Perisic wanted a state of emergency to be proclaimed because he thought using the army without that declaration was illegal?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: Basically, it is an illegal act; that is to say, a state of emergency would have to be proclaimed. And in the period when I was in active service, in Kosovo we did have a state of emergency in 1981. And we had to declare a state of emergency in 1989 in Kosovo, and that's when the army was used, together with other structures, with the MUP structures, at that time, the federal MUP; that is to say, that detachments came from Slovenia, Bosnia-Herzegovina, and other republics. And they were active in Kosovo, together with the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: It is in the absence of a state of emergency, what was the army's legitimate role in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: I did not understand you. It is well-known what the legitimate role of the army is. The army is always in the function of defending the territorial integrity of the country. So, specifically as far as Kosovo is concerned, the army had a priority task, to secure the state border towards Albania and neighbouring Macedonia.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could all other microphones be switched off when the witness is speaking. We have trouble hearing him.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. I will try to follow that direction from the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Around the same time that General Perisic and General Dimitrijevic had been replaced, we've heard evidence that Jovica Stanisic was replaced as well. Were you aware of that at the time?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: I am aware of that, but I don't know to what extent that is directly linked. As far as I know, first Jovica Stanisic was removed; if I'm not mistaken, that was sometime in the beginning of October 1998. And what later, Perisic was removed as well. Perisic was practically removed after his interview that he gave to some of the local media in Gornji Milanovac, the town of Gornji Milanovac, that he is from originally, where he openly said that he did not agree with the way that the army is being used in Kosovo, that a state of emergency should be declared. So he was practically removed after he went public. It was similar to the situation when I spoke publicly to the media, too; however, he was not pensioned off at the time. He was told that he should become assistant minister for national defence in the Ministry of Defence. Mr. Pavle Bulatovic was minister at the time. He refused that, and that is how he retired. General Dimitrijevic, when he was removed from the office he held, President Milosevic called him and told him that that was a very difficult office to hold and that he had held it for quite a while, and that he needed, well, a bit of a rest; and then he offered him another option, even to go somewhere as an ambassador. However, he refused that and he retired. He did not accept this rest.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I want to move on now and talk about --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I want to talk about the JNA and the VJ organisations and structures. You say in paragraph 7 of your statement, General, that during peacetime the body that was responsible for overall command of the JNA was the Supreme Defence Council. Do you know what the source of its authority was? Was that provided for in the law or on the constitution?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know again whether there was a mistake in the interpretation. What was it you said in the JNA period and then the expression the Supreme Defence Council was used. In the period when the JNA was still in existence when there was this collective Presidency of the SFRY that consisted of eight members --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you there, General. I'm concerned about 1998 and 1999. What body was in charge?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: The Supreme Defence Council and that is the Army of Yugoslavia then, not the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. My mistake. Do you know who the members were by law of the Supreme Defence Council?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I know that the Supreme Defence Council was headed by the president of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia; at that time it was Slobodan Milosevic; then, the permanent members were the presidents of the Republic of Serbia and Montenegro respectively. And from time to time, the Chief of General Staff and the minister of defence took part from time to time when they would be invited in the work of the Supreme Defence Council, but it was these three individuals that made up the Supreme Defence Council.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I would like to show the witness now Exhibit P1000.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: While we're waiting for that to come up. The Supreme Defence Council was the primary body during peacetime?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, I hope you'll have on your screen in a minute a document dated the 25th of December, 1998. It purports to be the minutes of the Supreme Defence Council on that date. Do you have that?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And can you look in the first paragraph under the heading -- minutes where it list the people attending. We see Mr. Milosevic as the chair, and the other persons attending are Mr. Milutinovic, the president of the Republic of Serbia; Mr. Djukanovic, the president of the Republic of Montenegro; Mr. Sainovic, the federal deputy prime minister; the defence minister Pavle Bulatovic, that you told us about; General Ojdanic, Chief of the General Staff; and General Susic, who appears to be the secretary of the Supreme Defence Council. Do you know what role Mr. Sainovic had in connection with the Supreme Defence Council?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: I think that Sainovic was the deputy prime minister of the federal government, if I'm not mistaken.
