utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Was there any provision in the law for him to be a member of the Supreme Defence Council that you're aware of -- that position, to be a member of the Supreme Defence Council?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I cannot interpret that part.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, again we're entering dangerous territory. General Vasiljevic said loud and clear two minutes ago that it is three individuals that make up the Supreme Defence Council, and then Mr. Hannis asks how Nikola Sainovic was a member of the Supreme Defence Council. Just look at the question he put. I'm trying to speak in principle, and I do not really want to interrupt anyone when speaking. I highly appreciate Mr. Vasiljevic. I have high regard for him, especially with regard to the period he spent in Croatia, but really, this is a meeting that he did not attend and a person who was not present there, now he is supposed to explain to you how Nikola Sainovic was a member of the Supreme Defence Council, which is something he never was and never will be. That is why we objected to the use of documents like these because they are being manipulated with.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I say something?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. The witness asked a question, Your Honour, but I wanted to say my question did not say that he was a member of the council. I asked what his role was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Vasiljevic, if a question is asked to which you do not know the answer, then you should tell us that you do not know. Now, do you consider that you are in a position to give us reliable evidence about the role of Mr. Sainovic at a meeting which took place when you were not in service?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, that's why I said what I said. I don't know whether you heard it, that I don't know, that I cannot interpret this other part I don't know. I know that these three key persons are members of the Supreme Defence Council; that is one thing. And the other thing I wanted to say in response to what the distinguished lawyer said. Nobody will make me say something I don't know. I will only speak about what I do know.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I want to apologise to you, and I -- that is why I said that I hold you in such high regard and I appreciate the work that you did, as I mentioned, and it is wrong for this to be done by the Prosecutor. That is my point. It really has nothing to do with you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I'm not in a position to say that what Mr. Hannis did was wrong. The witness was able to deal with the question and answered it clearly. The matter's over now and we can move on to something else. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. I would like to move to page 7 of the English of this document and page 10 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Before you do that, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I would like to ask the witness one question about paragraph 10 of the statement. Do you have the statement in front of you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have it. I just need to find the relevant page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: If you go to the end of paragraph 10 where you refer to other key VJ personnel, it's a question which will display my ignorance of army command structures, or at least a measure of confusion about them. You refer to two separate persons as respectively the chief of the 3rd Army -- sorry, my mistake. Two separate persons as respectively the commander of the Pristina Corps and the Chief of Staff of the Pristina Corps.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Are these positions, that's the commander of a corps or a body of the army, such as the Pristina Corps, are these two positions, commander and Chief of Staff, normally occupied by two separate individuals?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes, absolutely. These are two completely separate positions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Just in case there's any confusion in your mind, it's to resolve an issue that was raised in an entirely different context earlier in the trial. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, while we're there, I see what is a typographical error. General Stojimirovic is listed as chief of the 3rd Army, and I think it should be Chief of Staff of the 3rd Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General Vasiljevic, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And while we're on that can you explain the function of the Chief of Staff and his relationship to the commander of the Pristina Corps or the 3rd Army.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, every Chief of Staff is subordinated to his commander at all levels. As the word itself says, it is the Chief of Staff; that means that under him are other professional organs along the lines of different military activities; the infantry, the chief of infantry, the chief of artillery, the chief of signals, the traffic service, and so on and so forth. So this is an entire team that makes up the staff. The staff works on assessing the situation, preparing documents, decisions; whereas, the Chief of Staff is the main organiser of these activities. The Chief of Staff can also be considered, in a way, to be the deputy commander; this is to facilitate understanding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: When you get to the very top, though, the Chief of the General Staff is the most senior army officer, but the commander at that point is a political person. Is that correct? Or indeed a group of politicians?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. The Supreme Council of Defence is as a collective body that issues decisions on engaging the armed forces, and this they do through the staff, through the General Staff. In peacetime, it's General Staff that in keeping with state guidance relative to the army, in practical terms commands the army. And this pertain to the previous period. Now that the organisation has taken place, the re-organisation, the minister of defence is a member of a government, and his position is completely different with regard to the General Staff. Previously, the Chief of General Staff was directly linked to the president of the state, and now the Chief of General Staff is directly connected with the minister of defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That would suggest, though, that there's a distinction at the very top, that the commander and the Chief of Staff are the same at the top; whereas, in all the inferior army organisations, they are two different people. Is that the evidence you're giving?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me follow-up on that, if I may, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: During wartime, what body was the supreme body as far as commanding the army? Was it still the Supreme Defence Council?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: The Supreme Defence Council passes decisions, and the president of Yugoslavia, in the previous jargon that we used where there was the JNA in place, was the supreme commander. And in keeping with the decisions passed by the Supreme Defence Council, he passes those decisions to the Chief of General Staff, which in his turn passes down decisions on to the armed forces. This is my interpretation. However, in the Milosevic case, I also provided certain explanations and interpretations, but I believe that this should be done by somebody who is better versed in legal matters, who is familiar with the constitution, regulations, and laws. I know this only in principle, and what I can tell you is that the Supreme Defence Council passed decisions and the president of Yugoslavia, on behalf of the Supreme Defence Council, commands the army. And below him, there is a command structure headed by the Chief of Staff. In other words, the supreme commander, in that particular case President Milosevic, was not directly commanding over the corps, but he did that through the Chief of the General Staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Vasiljevic, just one point arising from that. Please look at paragraph 7 of your statement. In that paragraph, you say that during a state of war overall command lay with the Supreme Command; whereas, in peacetime it lay with a body with a different name, the Supreme Defence Council. Now, you seem to have contradicted that in what you've just said.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. No, I don't see any contradiction here. The Supreme Defence Council commands the armed forces in peacetime. In a state of war, however -- in a certain way, this is also the Supreme Command, and the supreme commander is the president of Yugoslavia. However, I believe that that part, at least I am not familiar with that part. I was not familiar with the constitution. And when I was reinstated, I didn't read the constitution. But I know that there were objections about Milosevic called the supreme commander, since there was no such position or function on paper. It only existed in the former Yugoslavia. I believe that legal experts will be better suited to explain that. I'm talking about the principle of the matter. The Supreme Defence Council was in command of the army in peacetime, and in a state of war it passed decisions; and in keeping with those decisions, the president of the republic had the overall command of the army, which means that the function of the Supreme Defence Council did not cease to exist if there was a state of war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, it sounds as though we don't have the right witness to deal with this, and I'm for the second time in this evidence now confused by the questions that are being asked to supplement the written evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I follow-up on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General Vasiljevic, during a time of war, did the General Staff of the army assume a different name? Was it still called the General Staff?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: It was the staff of the Supreme Command.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So I infer from that that there was some Supreme Command under which that staff was working. Do you know who the individuals were that made up the Supreme Command? I'm not talking about on paper; I'm talking about in real life.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: I'm only aware of the supreme commander, that was Milosevic. I don't know about the make-up of the Supreme Command. I don't know who the people were.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But you continued to use - in April of 1999 when you were reinstated - the term supreme commander was still used to refer to the individual who was giving direction to the army Supreme Command Staff?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And the Chief of Staff or the head of the Supreme Command Staff was General Ojdanic?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, let me return to this document that we were looking at minutes of the 8th Session of the Supreme Defence Council. On page 10 in the B/C/S, there is a reference to assignment to new duties in the Yugoslav army. Do you see that on page 10?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: I can't see the designation of the page, but I believe that I have the right page in front of me. It starts with the name, Ignjatovic, Dr. Aleksandar.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, and down below that do you see the heading: "Regulating the service status of generals, assignment to new duties in the Yugoslav army?"

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I have that before we.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If we could go to the next page in both the English and B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: When you were reinstated in April of 1999, do you know who the commander of the 3rd Army Corps was or the 3rd Army, I'm sorry?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: General Nebojsa Pavkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And commander of the Pristina Corps?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: General Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, this document says that General Lazarevic was the Chief of Staff of the Pristina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, and he's being moved to the position of the commander of the 3rd Army of Pristina Corps, if you'll read on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, in this meeting --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If we could go to page 9 of the English and page 13 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, I want to point you to a paragraph where the president of Montenegro, Mr. Djukanovic, is commenting on these proposed promotions and appointments. And do you see in the B/C/S the heading where his name is in bold?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And in the third paragraph under there, could you read that to us so that I can be sure that the English translation is correct? Can you read that third paragraph?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Would you read it out loud for us, please.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: "As far as the specific proposals are concerned, President Djukanovic did not wish to make any special comments. The more so that he only knew a few people personally. However, he did draw attention to the conflicting information coming from Kosovo in recent months regarding the engagement of the Pristina Corps. Information coming from Montenegro was often such that it indicated that the actions of the Pristina Corps were not always in accordance with the constitutional decision of the army and the decisions of the Supreme Defence Council. "If that is true, then the justification of the promotion of General Pavkovic, until now commander of the Pristina Corps, should be reconsidered, regardless of the fact that he does not doubt the evaluation that General Pavkovic has so far," and I don't see the rest of the sentence. That's the end of the sentence, and I believe that it goes on to say that he provided about Pavkovic's personality. "President Djukanovic pointed out that he would do everything in his power to have the Yugoslav Army follow the constitution of Yugoslavia again."

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, the next paragraph, and I think we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What's your question, Mr. Hannis?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I mean --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I could have read that for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: For one thing, Your Honour, I wanted to make sure my English translation was correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I understand that but I thought it was a preliminary to a question.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, it is. I think I have to address Mr. Milosevic's comment next to ask the question, because President Djukanovic suggested that there is some information he received in Monte Negro that the Pristina Corps had not been used properly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: President Milosevic in the next paragraph responds and says there had been no complaints about any illegal actions by the Pristina Corps, either from abroad or from inside. I think in your earlier answer you mentioned that General Perisic had complained about the use of the army in Kosovo; correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know what Mr. Djukanovic referred to, whether he had objections to the way the Pristina Corps was used and engaged. General Perisic did not have any objections about the engagement of the Pristina Corps, but the conditions under which it -- the army could be engaged, and the precondition was to proclaim a state of emergency. I see this document for the first time, but I can say that there were a lot of obstructions coming from Montenegro, from Mr. President Djukanovic towards President Milosevic and everything that was going on in Yugoslavia. I knew that at the time. And it is my feeling, if I may be allowed to share that with you, that this is just a direct opposition to Milosevic, rather than any principle matters dealing with the use of the army in Kosovo. This was their personal thing, the personal conflict that they had, that ended the way they did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now we have a real problem. That evidence is helpful to the Defence, as I see it. The Defence object to this sort of document being led through this witness. The witness wasn't involved in this at all. What he says may actually be mere speculation for all we know. We're really in territory, Mr. Hannis, that's not advancing the trial. This document may well be very relevant introduced in the right way or through the right person, but having a puppet in the witness box read it out to us is not going to advance the trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I regret that you're not seeing the purpose that I'm trying to accomplish here. The witness testified earlier that General Perisic was dismissed, and as I understood his testimony, part of that had to do with his disagreements about Mr. Milosevic failing to declare a state of emergency so the army can be used constitutionally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Djukanovic says he has some reservations about General Pavkovic being promoted; because as head of the Pristina Corps during his reign in Montenegro, he has heard complaints about the Pristina Corps actions not in accordance with the constitutional role of the army; then Mr. Milosevic says there have been no complaints. This is in December 25th, 1998.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's not a fair reflection of what the document says, Mr. Hannis. It says the army had been used -- let's go back -- we need to go back to the previous page. These are not -- the word in accordance with its constitutional role is not what I recollect Djukanovic as having said.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That's what it says in the English, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Let me see.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Maybe it wasn't translated that way when he read it; I thought it was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Oh, yes. Now, what I find difficulty with, Mr. Hannis, is understanding how reading this out assists us. We've heard what the witness has said about the view of Perisic. What use is it to have this witness read this out to us? Why should this not be presented as a document in some other way that we can read in due course in accordance with -- and compare with the evidence he can actually give? He's actually given evidence that suggests that Djukanovic was not being sincere here. He just had a personal grudge with Milosevic. So he's not advanced your position. The document might, but he hasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, to comment on this, I think I need to do it outside the presence of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Okay. I'm sorry about this, Mr. Vasiljevic, but I must ask you to leave the court briefly while we discuss a legal issue before resuming your evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honour, I think you may have seen already that this witness is protective of the army I think. I'm not saying that he's not testifying truthfully, but I think it's hard for him to take any position that he feels may reflect badly on the army. He testified earlier that General Perisic had disagreements with Mr. Milosevic and those were based in part on Perisic's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Hold on. Mr. O'Sullivan.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, the -- Mr. Hannis requested that the witness leave to discuss a legal issue. He's making comment here on what he believes the testimony is -- has been. I fail to see why we're even having this debate. There's no legal issue he's addressing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, he's explaining to me why he's approaching this, and I think it will be adequate if you respond once he's completed his submission, Mr. O'Sullivan. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. As I was saying, he had testified that General Perisic had disagreements with Mr. Milosevic, based in part on Perisic's concern that the army was being used in Kosovo in a way that was not consistent with the constitution and that he wanted Milosevic to declare a state of emergency so those troops could be used in something other than protecting the border, as they were being used. That non-constitutional role is what Mr. Djukanovic is complaining about, the same thing that General Perisic complained about. But when it comes from Djukanovic, this witness says he thinks he's prejudiced or biased. I then wanted to make the point that General Milosevic on the 25th of -- I mean Mr. Milosevic on the 25th of December, 1998, claims that there had been no complaints about illegal actions by the Pristina Corps when as early as July 1998 General Perisic, as we heard from Mr. Tanic and from the document that was introduced when he testified, General Perisic had written a letter to Mr. Milosevic complaining about that non-constitutional use of the army and how a state of emergency needed to be declared. Milosevic tells the Supreme Defence Council, "No, no, nobody every complained."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, I've got all that, Mr. Hannis. What I don't get is what is the take -- the relevance of the take of Mr. Vasiljevic on this. He's here as a puppet at the moment to read this out for you, and any comment he makes you'll say, "Well, that's because he's prejudiced in favour of the army. I just want him to read it out and want you, the Bench, to take a certain view of what he's read out." Now, that's not the way to deal with this type of evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I guess I want to be sure the Court was aware of these and I thought this was a good context to put it in, because we have a document pointing out who these Supreme Defence Council are and the matters they are dealing with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Was this one of the documents that you at some stage have asked us to accept as a free-standing document?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And why was it rejected?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I don't have the order in front of me. I don't --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, tell me what it is that Vasiljevic can add to the simple reading of the document by us alone.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: He can corroborate Mr. Tanic and General Perisic's letter that was challenged when it was introduced as a document that Perisic had complained about it before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You don't need the -- you don't need the minutes for that. You just need to ask the witness a question.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I want the minutes also to show, Your Honour, that Milosevic was lying about that to his own fellow members of the Supreme Defence Council.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And is that the extent of the use to which you intend to put this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. We want to put this document in for -- to show who the members of the Supreme Defence Council were, the matters that they dealt with. The last paragraph talks about how it is to be apprised of all matters regarding the army. It has to do with the chain of command and the authority over the army. And one other comment in this document, the very next one after general -- after Mr. Milosevic, is Mr. Milutinovic adding that some reports of lack of discipline and unconstitutional actions by the Pristina Corps were usually inflated, not false, but inflated. This is part of our argument, Your Honour, that the members of the joint criminal enterprise that we allege in this case were aware that the kinds of actions that they had been taking as far back as the summer of 1998 were in violation of the constitution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And what does Vasiljevic know about this?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The inflation of complaints?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, all -- as far as all I know is he knows General Perisic has complained about it, so there were complaints. I'm satisfied if the document is in evidence, Your Honours can read it. I can make my argument about what it means at the close of the case. But there -- as I understand it, there is a challenge to the authenticity of the document and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, there's been no specific that -- well, there may have been some specification of this one because it may not have a signature. Is this one of the unsigned documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: It has a signature and a seal, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It does.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: It's the seal of the secretary of the council, not Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, you must see that this witness adds to value to this particular document. What he does is give you evidence that can be related to the document and its contents. So we do not consider that he is the vehicle for the introduction of this or other similar documents. The -- this and other documents in the case may well be suitable for admission as free-standing documents in the circumstances we've now reached or through another witness. And they do appear to contain probative material, even as a simple example the sederunt of the meeting itself. But the witness is not going to add to that. So we ask you to re-consider your approach to this and deal with it differently and concentrate with the witness on things he can add value to from his own knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I will move on to another document. I do intend to continue asking him some questions about documents, and I hope that you will find that he does have helpful information as to those.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, we'll deal with that document as you ask questions of it, and in light of anything that's said by counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Fair enough, Your Honour, you used one term that I wasn't familiar with and I don't think the court reporter was either. It was a word to refer to the people in the meeting. Is it sederunt?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, that would be those sitting in the meeting. I meant to refer to the participants in the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can you spell that for us, I'm not familiar with it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's a Latin term, s-e-d-e-r-u-n-t.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Sorry. Shall we have the witness back in?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Vasiljevic, what we've been considering is whether it's appropriate for you to be asked questions about a document about which you appear to have no connection. It was because of that lack of connection I referred to you in this context as a puppet, but purely in that context. And what we've decided is that your lack of connection with this document means that it's not appropriate for the Prosecution to present this evidence through you. So we'll move on now to something else. A similar issue may arise, I warn you, but we'll deal with each issue as it arises in the context of your evidence. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And, General, I want to assure you the use of that term was no reflection on you, rather a reflection on me. I want to talk about your statement then at paragraph 7. We were still talking about the issue of the Supreme Command. In your statement you say, "During a state of war was the Supreme Command headed by Mr. Milosevic." And I know you're not an expert on this, but was it your understanding that the Supreme Command was made up of the same individuals who participated in the Supreme Defence Council?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, he's answered the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. O'Sullivan.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: The witness has answered that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: By saying?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: He said that he knew that there was only a supreme -- he's not an expert. He doesn't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: His knowledge was there was a supreme commander, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes. I think the witness has already disqualified himself from being able to answer that question in any different way than the answer he gave, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I need to move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I ask you, sir, in paragraph 8 you said: "During a state of war, members of the Supreme Command were dispersed to various locations in or near Belgrade." That seems to suggest there were more than one members of the Supreme Command. Who were you talking about there?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: First of all, I mean the staff of the Supreme Command. They were dispersed in different locations, and I spoke about that. The security administration was outside its command post, too. May I be of assistance now. In terms of my re-activation, it was President Milosevic who talked to me about it. I didn't see that there was anyone else that I knew. I knew Mr. Milutinovic. I knew Mr. Djukanovic. But absolutely after this controversial meeting that was shown to me here, I think that he no longer took part in meetings of the Supreme Defence Council. He obstructed them. Mr. Milutinovic, I did not see him. Whether he was at the locality where the Supreme Command Staff was, I don't know. And I'm talking about the staff of the Supreme Command that was dispersed in several different locations in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, the Supreme Command composition must be a constitutional matter. Do you not have a simple --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- extract from the constitution that answers that?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Because if you do, when we write the judgement, we'll not be referring to the evidence of Mr. Vasiljevic, we'll not be referring to the evidence of anyone else speculating about the composition of the Supreme Command or the Supreme Defence Council, we'll be looking at the law.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And if the law has been deviated from, we'll be looking at the facts that demonstrate that it wasn't operated the way it was supposed to be operated. But to ask this witness what the theory was is not advancing the case. That's what I read paragraph 7 to be.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I didn't believe I was asking him a question about the theory. I was asking him what members of the Supreme Command Staff referred to or members of the Supreme Command. I take your point, but it is our argument, Your Honour, that with regard to some things what appeared in the law and on paper was not the reality on the ground. And, in some cases, I'm trying to give you both versions; what is in the law and what people on the ground saw and experienced.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General Vasiljevic, which representative of the security services attended daily Supreme Command Staff meetings? Who was that?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: At the time when I came, and after that, I know what the situation was. Most often these meetings that were held in the evening were attended by Colonel Gajic, and in addition to him Colonel Radicanin and another colonel. So usually it was three colonels from the security administration who came to these meetings. Very seldom General Geza Farkas would come, only every now and then.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you ever attend any of those briefings?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, you also say that there was one security duty officer at the Supreme Command Staff command post. Who did that -- well, first of all, let me ask you: Did you ever do that duty?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: It wasn't a security duty officer. As for the security of the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia, there was a department of security for the General Staff, and that department was partly deployed at the command post where the staff of the Supreme Command was.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, although you didn't personally attend any of the daily Supreme Command Staff meetings, were you informed about the content of these briefings?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, usually at morning meetings at the security administration, we would briefly be given information from that evening briefing that could pertain to security problems. So it was not regular practice that what was discussed in the evening at the staff of the Supreme Command, that on the next day we at the security administration would be informed about that. It was dealt with on a case-by-case basis and problem-by-problem basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could we show the witness Exhibit Number 2601.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, in your statement in paragraph 14, you make reference to this chart as depicting the organisational structure of the major VJ units associated with Kosovo in 1999. Can you see that on your screen now?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: I can see it for the most part.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do we need to enlarge it?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: If possible, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And is that an accurate reflection of the structure and the chain of command within the army down to the units in Kosovo in 1999?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: Only part of the units are depicted here, of course, so this diagram as it stands is correct for the most part.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: When you say "only part of the units," are you referring to the subordinate units under the command of the Pristina Corps that are not fully reflected?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But as for the chain at the Pristina Corps level and above, is it complete and accurate?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, it goes towards the command of the 3rd Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. In paragraph 15, you discuss the chain of command and how orders would be created and sent down the line. And in paragraphs 16 to 18 related to that, you talk about the flow of information and reporting. What kinds of reports would subordinate units in the field, like the brigades under the Pristina Corps, what kind of reports would they make in April of 1999 during the combat in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: What I'm saying now is based on the practice that I'm aware of in the army in general, not only in the Pristina Corps but also throughout the chain of command. And I assume that, therefore, this mechanism existed in the Pristina Corps, too. So brigades, specifically in response to this question, brigades submit daily combat reports to the corps command. These are regular reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And based on your long experience in the JNA and the VJ, did those reports have a specific format that was to be followed in creating a daily combat report?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, there were questions that had to be included in that combat report. The content was prescribed in terms of what would be entered into the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can you recall some of those specific topics?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: On the whole, it pertained to knowledge about enemy activities, then the results of engaging our own forces, then problems within units, problems in the territory, and then there are proposals, conclusions about activities concerning the following day. So generally speaking, that is regular combat reports, but also there would be additional reports about extraordinary events that would take place. They could be submitted a bit later, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can you give us an example of an extraordinary event that would result in a separate report being created and sent up the line.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, extraordinary events are events that are not regular in terms of the way activities evolve. For example, an extraordinary event could be, say, that a crime had been committed that was learned of subsequently or if an event would happen in the territory that would affect combat activities and the morale of the said unit. So something from the previous period could also be written about if it would merit attention, that particular event. And, also, a special report could have been sought. The superior command could have been asked for a special report on a special problem. So it would not be dealt with in the regular report but in a separate report.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But the fact that it was reported in a separate report would not exclude it from being also included in a regular combat report. Is that right? For example, if there had been an incident between members of the army and civilians in which civilians were injured or killed, that would be the subject of an extraordinary report, but it would -- would it also go in a regular daily combat report?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, it should and usually it would be under a particular item that was called "other events," and then that would include descriptions of things that were not regular events, if I can call them that. So under these other events, such events could be described.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Who was responsible for writing--

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Who was responsible for writing and sending these reports up the chain of command?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: These reports are sent by the commander and they bear his signature, and the report is prepared by his staff. When the commander is absent, then the person who stands in for him, who he decides will stand in for him. In most cases, it is the Chief of Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, did all of these individual reports go all the way up the chain of command or did they only go to the next level? How did that work? For example, on the chart we have a subordinate brigade to the Pristina Corps. A report from that brigade goes to Pristina Corps. What happens next?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: That means that the system of reporting goes all the way up to the staff of the Supreme Command, and then the staff of the Supreme Command also writes its daily operations report, as it is called. So it goes all the way up the vertical chain. Events that are included in reports at higher levels are appropriately selected, of course. So a report that was submitted by a brigade would not go all the way up to the staff of the supreme defence -- the Supreme Command. They would not copy out the entire report of that brigade. So the relevant data have to be selected all the way up.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So someone at the Pristina Corps then would take all of those daily reports from the subordinate brigades and condense that information into a single report, which was sent up to the 3rd Army?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And then the 3rd Army, I take it, would take reports from its subordinates, likewise condense it into a single report, and send it up to the -- during the time of war, up to the Supreme Command Staff?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, the staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned I think in your testimony earlier that each unit, for example, each battalion would have assigned to it a security officer. Did security officers also generate their own reports, separate and apart from the one prepared by the commander of the brigade, the daily combat report? Did they have a separate reporting system?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: They have their own reporting system; however, when lower levels of command are concerned, for example, in a battalion or a brigade, then the security officer takes some of his knowledge that is of interest to the combat-readiness of the unit that he is in. That would be attached to the daily combat report. That is one thing. As for the vertical chain, at lower levels of command, they were not duty-bound to write regular, daily operations reports; that is to say that down the vertical of the security organs, they sent their reports, depending on the volume of information they would obtain. However, the command of the armies and their security people were duty-bound to submit reports on a daily basis. And they would receive information from all subordinated security organs within the army, depending on who had what kind of information; and then at the level of the army of the security department of the army, they would select, filter these -- this information that was gathered, and then it would go to the security administration as such. At its own level, the security administration worked on its daily reports, including the reports of military police units that were down the professional line subordinated to the security administration. So that report to the security administration would be provided to the staff of the Supreme Command. However, what the Presiding Judge said a few moments ago, that then it was even more unclear to him as to what it was that the security organ reported on. These daily reports of the security organs that went to the operations centre of the supreme commander or the staff of the Supreme Command, they included general events relevant to security. It's quite hard for me to explain what kind of events these are. But as far as counter-intelligence is concerned, only the Chief of Staff of the Supreme Command would receive that kind of information, or rather the Chief of General Staff, who according to the law is in charge of the counter-intelligence part of the work of the organs. So the security administration worked on these reports and sometimes on specific daily reports, for example, with regard to foreign agents or the like.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Let me follow-up on that, but first I have to go back for a moment to the, for example, the daily combat reports from the units that went up the line. And you said once it got to the 3rd Army, it would prepare a report, summarising and condensing the reports it had from its subordinates that went to the staff of the Supreme Command. From there, were there any reports prepared by the Supreme Command Staff that went further up the line to the supreme commander?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: The staff of the Supreme Command wrote daily operative reports that were submitted to some organs within the General Staff. So, this daily operations report from the Supreme Command Staff also came to the security administration, and then we would see in the briefest possible terms what had happened, say, in the 3rd Army, the 2nd Army, the 1st Army. And in all other directly subordinated units, the units subordinated to the staff of the Supreme Command, as far as I know, such a report would also go to President Milosevic as the supreme commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, is this an appropriate time for the break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Mr. Hannis. We have to break again, Mr. Vasiljevic, this time for half an hour. We'll be resuming at 10 minutes to 1.00. If you could meanwhile please go with the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, before I move on to another topic, I wanted to ask you a couple more questions about the security organs attached to the units in the field and up the chain of command. You've explained to us about the counter-intelligence aspect of security work, and I understand that to involve trying to deal with foreign intelligence services and their activities and the enemies of the VJ. But the security side of the house, the non-counter-intelligence part, what kinds of things was it involved in investigating? Can you give us some examples.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: Again, are we talking about the counter-intelligence sector or the prevention sector? Do you want a specific example of what was investigated?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That would help me.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: I can talk about espionage.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No, I don't want to know about espionage. What kinds of threats to the army did the security service investigate other than from foreign agents, from outside the army? Did it also investigate internal threats?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: The security service has its methodology that it uses. One part of it were sources, people who exist in units, on the territory, in various points where the enemy activity might be expected. Every information that the security officer obtains working with his sources - and that is not directly linked with the espionage activities, a terrorist organisation, but still might have an impact on the overall combat-readiness and the morale of the troops - is what they will report to their commanders about. For example, if you know what the obligations were with regard to the crimes and other negative things that took place in Kosovo, if the security officer obtained such information, he would report on those to his commander. If serious -- more serious things were involved, then they would be duty-bound to report to the superior security organ; in other words, he had to report both to the commander of his unit and his superior commander along the lines of security.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me take an example of a brigade in Kosovo. What was the typical rank held by a commander of a brigade?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: Either a colonel or a lieutenant-colonel waiting to be promoted into the rank of colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And the security officer assigned to a brigade, what -- typically what rank would he hold?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: Most commonly major or captain first class.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And, for example, in a case where the major or the captain, the security officer, in a brigade had information that the commander, the colonel or the lieutenant-colonel, may have been involved in something that involved a crime, killing of civilians, or his men or looting and he wasn't doing anything about it, would the major, the security officer -- how would he handle that? It wouldn't make any sense for him to report it to the commander if he thought the commander were involved. So what would he do?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: He would send the information to the security organ in the corps and that would be his superior along the professional line; and then the security organ in the corps would inform the corps commander about that, and then measures would be passed down along the command line to effect the perpetrator.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Would the commander of the corps who received that information, what was his responsibility in terms of dealing with the suspected brigade commander? Was he to inform him of the allegations or was he to report it up the line to the army or both?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: It all depends on the case. As a matter of principle, the corps commander could require from the security organ to collect additional information about the whole case, the operations information. However, if there is enough of such information, then the corps commander can call the commander of the brigade and ask him to report to him or he can set up a commission that will deal with that breach of discipline. If the alleged breach has -- is of the criminal nature, then he would have to inform the judiciary bodies that would in their turn instigate a full investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I want to move on to paragraph 18 of your statement. You indicate in addition to these reports that worked their way up to the Supreme Command Staff and General Ojdanic, that General Ojdanic sometimes -- or he or his superiors -- subordinates would sometimes send professional teams to the field. What kind of teams were sent out to the field and for what purposes?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: It was to control or extend assistance to the subordinated commands. Control groups were sent along various lines. For example, a control could be sent to check the morale of the troops. We also sent controls to check the security situation and to extend assistance to the security organs in the lower-ranking units. I went on such a control inspection with General Gajic. Such groups were sent across the sectors, and there were such controls that were sent by General Ojdanic on several occasions every time to deal with different issues. In -- it was mostly to do with the activities of the army, like command structure signals or looking at the overall structure of the army and how it functioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, may we go into private session for one minute. I want to go into paragraph 20 of his statement where there is a portion that he's asked to address in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's to ensure that anyone identified is not publicly identified. Is that --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well. We shall do that.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, we're back in open session now. In paragraph 19 of your statement, you mention that "the chain of command was often circumvented by General Pavkovic going directly to Milosevic without the knowledge or authorisation of General Ojdanic." Can you give us some examples of that.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: An example of that took place in mid-June when I arrived at the White Palace to see Milosevic with General Ojdanic. We were there early, a few minutes before the beginning of the meeting; and while we were waiting in the car, we saw General Pavkovic leaving the White Palace. He had obviously met up with President Milosevic, and then General Ojdanic told me, "See him, see him. He is seeing Milosevic again and he never reported to me before that." I know that he is here very often and that he tells a lot more to Sainovic than he tells me. This is the concrete conversation and the concrete event that transpired that day. I knew from 1998 that General Pavkovic spent some time in Belgrade. On several occasions, and according to him, he had been in touch with President Milosevic and Mr. Sainovic. When we arrived at Milosevic's office to discuss the existing problem, General Ojdanic said to Milosevic -- actually, he asked him not to call his subordinates without his knowledge. Milosevic said, "Well, you know, he was here not in an official capacity. He just dropped by." In other words, Ojdanic did draw Milosevic's attention to that, and when we returned he told me that Pavkovic had had several contacts with Milosevic and that neither Milosevic nor Pavkovic ever bothered to tell him about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Was this the first time that General Ojdanic had mentioned this problem to you?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: That was the first time. Before that I had never had an opportunity to discuss unofficial matters with General Ojdanic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. In paragraph 21 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Before moving on, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is the part at the beginning of that paragraph, 20, of no significance in fact? It's just there, or is there some significance in that meeting that led to the witness being invited to the White Palace?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, we've heard testimony from another witness relating to the named individual and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So there is some significance in this? It's not just there as an explanation for him being at the White Palace?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, in paragraph 21 of your statement, General, you mention that when Pavkovic was commander of the Pristina Corps in 1998, he dealt directly with Milosevic, bypassing two levels in the chain of command. How did you know about this? This was before your activation in April 1999. What's your source of information about that?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: The source of my information are two retired highly ranking officers of the JNA with whom I had frequent contacts. We socialised, and they in their turn were in contact with Colonel Pavkovic. And when I spoke to these two friends of mine, they would tell me that Pavkovic was there, that he had spoken with Milosevic and Sainovic about the use of army in Kosovo. So this is my indirect knowledge based on what they told me, and not only them but also some other colleagues of mine. And on one occasion - and I believe it was in autumn 1998 - I met up with Mr. Pavkovic who was together with those two retired officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you have any conversation with him at that time?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but the topic of this conversation was not his visits to Milosevic. He was interested in what I knew about some officers who were supposed to be appointed to high positions in the security administration. A colleague of mine and I who were there provided him with the information about these two officers and gave him our evaluation. I don't want to mention their names. But he would often say that he was with Sainovic and Milosevic, and on that occasion he did mention, just in passing, that he had been in contact with them. However, whether he reported to his superior officers that he had been in contact with those two in 1998, I don't know. But I know that he did come there frequently and that he was in touch with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: One thing in that answer. You said, Mr. Vasiljevic, that a colleague of yours and you provided him the information about two officers; and then you said: "But he would often say that he was with Sainovic and Milosevic." Now, you only met him -- you only had this discussion on one occasion with Pavkovic. Is that correct? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I was with Pavkovic only once, but I had several contacts with the two retired officers who --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, are you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- had told me that they had been with Pavkovic, that Pavkovic had visited Milosevic, Sainovic, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That clarifies that. Are you going to tell us who these two officers were or is there some reason why we're not going into that, Mr. Hannis?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, are those names that you are willing to mention in private session?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could we go into private session, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And indeed why that basic fact wasn't brought out because it makes a difference to the status of the evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I didn't know the status of those two gentlemen, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. We're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Let's clarify this. Is there a good reason why that evidence should have been given in private session, bearing in mind what you've just said about what's happened to these two persons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because I am on very good terms with their families, and it is not a good thing to mention them in public. I'm still in contact with their respective families.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, that wouldn't be an adequate reason for it being done in private that it's just not a good thing. What are you saying would be the implications for them of having it mentioned in public?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know whether they would agree with me mentioning their names in public.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: May I ask a question of the general in that regard, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, do you have some concerns that there would be some sort of repercussions against the family members if those names had been mentioned?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I have no other questions, Your Honour, on that topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, paragraph 20 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Sorry. My silence was because I was in thought, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Would anyone from the Defence care to assist us on this one? Is there anyone particularly concerned that this evidence should be in public -- in the public domain? Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I support the general's positions because you have to know the situation in our country, and I don't think that it would be pleasant for the deceased persons to be mentioned in open and the families would not take it lightly, and that is our problem and that's why I would like to support Mr. Vasiljevic's position not to mention the names of these people in public. You have to be aware of the customs in our country.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, in the exceptional circumstances and on compassionate grounds and bearing in mind what's been said by Mr. Fila without any contradiction from any other source, we will in this one instance retain the private session status of that passage of the evidence. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, still in paragraph 21 of your statement, you also say that General Pavkovic may have earned Milosevic's favour in 1998 when he, Pavkovic, was willing to use the VJ in Kosovo, in contrast to General Perisic who was reluctant and who wanted a state of emergency declared first. How did you know -- what was your source of information that Pavkovic was willing to use the VJ in Kosovo in a way that Perisic was not?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, these are generally known things over there in our part of the world. The pensioning of General Perisic is something that he publicly spoke about in the press, the interview that I referred to earlier on. The fact that Pavkovic enjoyed President Milosevic's support remains. According to the knowledge that I know, even his promotion to a higher rank did not go through usual procedure. He just told those who were present that he had been promoted to a higher rank and that they can congratulate him. Am I supposed to mention names now in open session? I can, but I must say that I came to into this entire situation as an individual who was speaking about all of this, and I was threatened earlier on about -- because of things I said. And I can say exactly who it was who told me about this. Secondly, in an indirect way, he was related to the Milosevic family through his wife, who had family ties to Mira Markovic. So in terms of that relationship, the general belief was - and those were the stories that were bandied about - that it is on that account, on account of that relationship, that he enjoyed the great confidence of the Milosevics.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. That was the next question I was going to ask you. I don't intend to ask you the names that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, that's a matter for you, Mr. Hannis, in this instance. What concerns me more is that this is all very well in isolation as an example perhaps of an allegation of favouritism. But on the ground in Kosovo, can you give us an example of what the army did that Perisic, for example, would not have tolerated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perisic did not accept using the army without declaring a state of emergency. He was not opposed to using the army in Kosovo, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I understand that. Give me an example of what the army actually did that they shouldn't have done and that he wouldn't have allowed them to do.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know of an example where Mr. Pavkovic ordered something that he had not been allowed to order. So I cannot go into that and I cannot go into assumptions as to what Perisic would have done. I just know that the line of discord was between Milosevic and Perisic, and in that situation Pavkovic came to the surface and that was refusal to use the army in Kosovo without declaring a state of emergency. I cannot go into assumptions now as to what he would have done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Vasiljevic, the army were entitled to be in Kosovo, as the army are entitled to be on the land of any part of the world to which they belong. What I'm interested in is what was it that they did. Leaving aside for the moment who ordered it, what was it the army did in Kosovo that they ought not to have done without a state of emergency being declared, which we can then assume Perisic would not have allowed to happen? Give me an example of something they actually did that they could only do if a state of emergency had been declared.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Again, we haven't understood each other. What he is not allowed to do if a state of emergency is not declared, do I understand you properly? He cannot take the troops out of barracks. He cannot use armoured brigades that would support MUP forces in fighting the terrorist groups in Kosovo if a state of emergency had not been declared, according to which the army can be used for carrying out such tasks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And do you know of examples where these things happened, where the armoured brigades were used in support of MUP forces and troops were taken out of barracks when they should not have been?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I learned about that later. I cannot say specifically now what the time was when this happened; but at any rate when I was re-activated, then I did have knowledge that these units were operating down there and being used down there. I also had knowledge from -- from when I went to the security administration in 1998 and the reaction of General Dimitrijevic to the fact that the army was being taken out of the barracks and the MUP was being supported, although the state of emergency had not been declared. Now I've used his name, that I heard about that from him, and there were these reactions with regard to this problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Presumably, the reference you made to the period when you had been re-activated was during a state of war, and therefore the circumstances had changed by then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I said just now I'll have to speak slowly. I think that in the second half of 1998, and there was no war on then --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I understood that --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- in the security administration --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But you said that: "When I was re-activated, then I did have knowledge that these units were operating down there and being used down there." Were you, in saying that, referring back to 1998?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. When I was re-activated in 1999 and when I went to Kosovo, and when I was briefed by the security organs, then I learned even more details than I had from when I went to see people in the security administration in 1998. So when I came there to Kosovo, I was only told about this in greater detail.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, to follow up on that point, could we show the witness Exhibit P1427, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, do you have that on the screen in front of you now?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Actually, if I may, Your Honour, to save time, if I could have the usher hand him a hard copy of this document. It may save some time in turning pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: This is from the Pristina Corps command. It appears to be signed by General Pavkovic and sealed from the 10th of August, 1998, entitled, A Decision on Joint Engagement of the MUP and VJ Forces. Could you look at item number 2.5 under the task for units and tell us if that's an example of what you were telling the Judges about before, about armoured units in support of MUP.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: I could not say that this is an example of engaging armoured units in this particular paragraph, because BG15-3, that is not an armoured group. To the best of my knowledge 2/1 is an armoured, that is BG-52 is that one -- no, sorry, 252 is an armoured brigade; however, this one is not an armoured brigade and 15/3 is the 15th Brigade from Pristina as far as we know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The same thing. The general is looking at a document that he's never seen, and now he's being asked to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, I understand the point you're going to make but there is a difference here.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What's happening is that the witness has described the circumstances which are necessary for -- or the effect of a declaration of a state of emergency, and what Mr. Hannis is trying to do is identify in this document through him something that might require the declaration of a state of emergency. Now, he's entitled to ask the witness something that happened even when he wasn't in the army satisfies what he describes as necessary. And that's all that's happening, and therefore I don't think you can object to this particular question.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's not what I objected to. I'm objecting to the detailed analysis as to the units that had been used. At the beginning of his answer, he said that this was not a good example. He's already said that, and now he is being asked to go into all this detail. This is part of the objection. As for the first bit, I agree with you on that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... Mr. Fila. Now, Mr. Hannis, can you ask another question to focus this issue, because the one you did ask has been answered.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I need to follow up on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, will you look at the end of the document under General Pavkovic's signature to the distribution list, and my English translation refers to the 15th OKBR, which is translated here as armoured brigade. Does that refresh your recollection about the nature of the 15th?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: This does not refresh my recollection. That is the 15th Armoured Brigade. BG15-3, I can only assume that it referred to a combat group from the 15th Armoured Brigade. Now, whether tanks had actually been used or not is something I don't know. An armoured brigade does not only have tanks, but it also has mechanised APCs and other equipment. You asked whether tanks had been used and I cannot say either yes or no.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, would you look at item 5.1 under technical support, and it lists the following quantity of ammunition and the third item is: "Ammunition for tanks." Would not that suggest that indeed tanks had been intended to be used in this operation?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, then this paragraph confirms that and proves that tanks were used. But the other paragraph that you referred me to, 2.5, is something that did not make it obvious.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I understand. And at paragraph 2.5 indicates that the battle group from the 15th Armoured Brigade is to attack along with the 7th MUP detachment; correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: No, it doesn't say 15th Brigade. It says combat group of the 15th Brigade-3. So that is only part of the 15th Brigade. How big a part of the brigade, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You're right, I misspoke. I should have said "battle group." Okay. Now, let me go back and pick up where we were. We just finished talking about General Pavkovic. I want to move now to paragraph 25 through 27 of your statement where you're talking about volunteers and the VJ. Did you ever hear of a group called the Phantoms in connection with the VJ?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: I did not hear of any Phantoms. I do not recollect any such thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In paragraph 26, you mention that there were specific orders on who can be a volunteer and how. It's correct, isn't it, that there were restrictions on volunteer units, that volunteers could only come into the army as individuals, rather than a whole unit coming in as a volunteer unit.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That had not been the situation in 1991 and 1992, had it?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: In 1992 and 1991, the situation was quite different; it wasn't like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And is it because - at least in part - because of some of the problems with crimes committed by volunteer units in the conflicts in Croatia and Bosnia that the rules changed for volunteers coming into the army?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: The only thing I know from the period when I was re-activated and when I was expressing particular interest in possible problems with volunteers is that I saw that organisationally and in terms of regulations that question had been resolved well. Two collection centres were set up as far as the Army of Yugoslavia was concerned for taking in volunteers. One centre was in Grocka near Belgrade and the other one was in Medja near Nis. And the volunteers went through check-ups, security clearance; and according to the information I had, about 50 percent of the volunteers who had applied did not meet these criteria and were not admitted into the Army of Yugoslavia. After this selection process in the centre for taking in volunteers, their training was organised and then they were sent on to units. In units, there were already orders by the staff of the Supreme Command in terms of how they should be taken in, and it was strictly forbidden for them to be taken in as groups, rather, they could only be admitted individually based on the specialty each one of them had.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But you were aware that there indeed had been problems with volunteers and paramilitaries in Croatia and Bosnia in 1991 through 1992?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Next I want to go to paragraph 28 where you talk about the MUP and its -- and its organisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, there is a brief section that the witness had wished to address in private session. I wonder if we could do that now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Again to do with identity, is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, and I think he does have a legitimate concern about the name in question this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honour, I'm actually about to move on to a new area. I wonder if this might be an appropriate occasion to break for the day. I know it's a couple minutes early.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Hannis. Mr. Vasiljevic, that brings our session for today to an end. We will resume tomorrow at 9.00, when you should be here to continue your evidence. It's important that overnight, that's tonight and any other overnight or over the weekend that you're still with us, that you don't discuss any part of your evidence with any person at all; and by that I mean by either the evidence you've already given or the evidence you're about to give in the case. You can talk about anything else with anybody you like, but you mustn't talk with anyone at all, official or unofficial or anyone, about the evidence itself. So please leave the courtroom now with the usher and we will see you again tomorrow at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: 9.00 tomorrow.
